background.definition: Aplastic anemia is a disorder where myeloid progenitor and stem cells are severely diminished or absent in the bone marrow, which leads to pancytopenia.

list.listitem: Two cases per million in Western countries
Five to 6 cases per million in Asian countries
There is a biphasic age distribution with one peak in the teens and early 20s and a second peak in the elderly.

For patients with Fanconi anemia, a rare, inherited blood disorder leading to bone marrow failure, endocrine disorders are common (80%) and include growth hormone (GH) deficiency, abnormal glucose or insulin metabolism, dyslipidemia, hypothyroidism, pubertal delay, infertility, and hypogonadism.

Aplastic anemia is closely associated with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), an acquired blood disease caused by somatic mutations in the phosphatidylinositol glycan class A gene. Very small (approximately 10 to 50 per million) polyclonal populations of PNH cells can be detected in most healthy individuals and about one third of patients with PNH clones have classic PNH with hemolysis.

Aplastic anemia is also associated with eosinophilic fasciitis, also called Shulman disease. This rare sclerodermiform syndrome can present with swelling and pain in the extremities, thickened skin, muscle weakness and bone pain.
Etiologies of aplastic anemia vary widely. Most cases are idiopathic. Other causes include exposure to various drugs, infections, and radiation.
Genetics: Fanconi anemia, a DNA-repair disorder, may be linked to mutations in ubiquitin ligase RFWD3 and HLA-A/B/DRB1. Interferon gamma polymorphisms appear to play a role in aplastic anemia.
Drugs: Chloramphenicol, gold, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and multiple chemotherapeutic regimens are associated with aplastic anemia.
Viruses: Specific viral agents associated with aplastic anemia include parvovirus B-19, Epstein-Barr virus, and HIV.
Pregnancy has also been associated with aplastic anemia.

Sporadic aplastic anemia is an immune-mediated disease. Molecular and cellular pathways have been mapped in detail for the effector cell, T lymphocyte and target cells, and the progenitor or hematopoietic stem cell.

Antigens are presented to T lymphocytes by antigen-presenting cells, possibly by the HLA-B allele, causing proliferation and activation of the T cells. This activation leads to a cascade, resulting in reduced cell cycling and hematopoietic cell death by apoptosis.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 studies including 4428 patients found evidence suggesting that HLA-DRB1*0301 decreased the risk of aplastic anemia while HLA-DRB1*0901 and HLA-DRB1*1501 were risk factors for the disease.
Autoimmune suppression of glycosylphosphatidylinositol-positive hematopoietic stem cells has been identified in many patients with idiopathic aplastic anemia.
Other pathologies resulting in an empty bone marrow include direct toxins such as chemotherapy, irradiation or industrial chemicals and constitutional syndromes including germline mutations.
In one study of 439 patients with aplastic anemia, somatic mutations in myeloid cancer candidate genes were present in one third of the patients and some mutations were related to clinical outcomes.

In patients with severe aplastic anemia treated with haplo-identical HCT, mesenchymal stromal cells do not appear to reduce risk of graft-versus-host disease or improve survival based on a meta-analysis of 29 single-arm studies, 8 combined with mesenchymal stromal cells, including 1456 patients.
Patients typically present with vague or diffuse symptoms such as bleeding, shortness of breath, and generalized weakness. C
CBC will show pancytopenia. C
Bone marrow biopsy and peripheral smear are necessary to classify the severity of the aplastic anemia and rule out other causes of pancytopenia. C
Aplastic anemia may be further classified into moderate, severe, and very severe ().
Aplastic anemia may present with signs and symptoms common for pancytopenia.
Bleeding is the most common early symptom. Easy bruising, oozing from gingiva, epistaxis, heavy menstrual flow, and petechiae may also occur due to thrombocytopenia.
Anemia may present with increasing weakness and shortness of breath.
Infection is an atypical presenting symptom in patients with aplastic anemia.
A CBC is the initial diagnostic test of choice. If pancytopenia is found, order a peripheral smear and reticulocyte count.
Peripheral smears typically show large erythrocytes with minimal platelets and granulocytes. Reticulocytes are usually absent and lymphocyte numbers may be normal or reduced.

PNH clones, also called "escape clones," are red or white blood cells that entirely or partially lack glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored proteins (GPI-linked antigens) on the cell surface. These clones are evidence of acquired immune-mediated bone marrow failure and have a high prevalence in patients with aplastic anemia. Authors of a meta-analysis of 11 cohort studies with 1236 patients found presence of PNH clones vs. absence was a positive predictor of response to immunosuppression treatment at 6 months (OR 2.85, 95% CI 2.17-3.75). There was no difference between groups in early mortality.

Confirm the diagnosis with a bone marrow biopsy. In aplastic anemia, biopsy will show dramatic hypocellularity with fatty infiltration while the remaining hematopoietic cells stay morphologically normal.

Genomic screening for the approximately 50 genes that cause constitutional marrow failure can be valuable but adds to cost and can produce results of uncertain significance. It may be particularly useful for children (see below) and when myelodysplastic syndromes are suspected.
A high index of suspicion is needed to diagnose aplastic anemia. Patients typically present with vague symptoms including generalized weakness, bleeding, and shortness of breath.
A CBC, peripheral smear, and bone marrow biopsy are necessary for definitive diagnosis.
Hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) is the definitive therapy; it is limited by availability of an HLA-matched donor and age and /or fitness of the patient. B
Supportive care with transfusions of platelets and blood as needed as well as treatment of infections and antimicrobial prophylaxis are important throughout the patient's course of treatment. C
Immunosuppressive therapies do not provide cures but can result in an improved prognosis. B
Anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) in combination with cyclosporine is the immunosuppressive therapy of choice in patients not able to tolerate HCT. B
Eltrombopag when added to ATG and cyclosporine increases the likelihood of treatment response at 3 months (NNT = 4) and is recommended by British Society for Hematology guidelines (2024). B
Immunosuppressive therapies do not provide cures but can result in an improved prognosis.

ATG, also known as thymoglobulin, is an immune globulin therapy made of polyclonal antibodies against human T cells that is first-line therapy in aplastic anemia. For a single treatment course, dosing is 40 mg per kilogram per day IV for 4 days. The drug is administered over 4-6 hours and the patient should be premedicated with corticosteroids, acetaminophen, and/or antihistamines to prevent complications.

In a case series from Europe and Asia of 955 people with aplastic anemia treated with ATG as first-line treatment, actuarial 10-year survival was 70% and transplant free survival was 64%. Negative predictors of survival in multivariate analysis, were greater severity of the disease, older age and longer interval between diagnosis and treatment.

Cyclosporine can be used in conjunction with ATG. Blood levels of cyclosporine between 200 and 500 ng/mL are suitable for optimal treatment. This therapy is generally continued for 6 months with maintenance therapy based on blood levels and side effect profile.

Sources for ATG are horse and rabbit. In a retrospective study, overall survival and failure-free survival were not significantly different between the two, although complete response was more rapid with horse ATG. However, in a RCT, horse ATG plus cyclosporine was clearly superior to rabbit ATG plus cyclosporine in both hematologic response at 6 months (68% vs. 37%, respectively) and overall 3-year survival (96% vs. 76%, respectively).
Eltrombopag (Promacta)

Eltrombopag (EPAG) is a thrombopoieitin receptor agonist that appears to have a direct effect on marrow stem cells. It is available in oral form for use for 6 months and, for first-line therapy, is dosed at 150 mg once daily for adults and adolescents, 75 mg once daily for children aged 6-11 years and 2.5 mg/kg mg once daily for children aged 2-5 years. The drug is initiated in patients already taking ATG and cyclosporine A. For patients with relapsed or refractory severe aplastic anemia, dosing starts at 50 mg once daily.

In a randomized trial with 197 patients comparing standard therapy with ATG + cyclosporine versus standard therapy plus EPAG, the overall treatment response was significantly higher in the combined therapy group at 3 months (59% vs 31%, NNT = 4) and at 6 months (68% vs. 41%). Adverse events were similar between groups.

Authors of systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 retrospective studies and 4 RCTs, with a total of 1,264 patients, comparing ATG combined with EPAG with ATG alone found a higher effective rate (odds ratio [OR] 1.90, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.35 to 2.68) and survival rate (OR 2.54, 95% CI 1.58 to 4.09) with combined treatment. Interestingly, side effects were lower in the combined therapy group.

However, authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs including 542 patients with aplastic anemia found a higher 6-month complete response with adjunctive EPAG (OR 2.2, 95% CI 1.5-3.1), but with significantly increased pigment deposition and abnormal liver function with EPAG combined with immunosuppressive therapy compared to immunosuppressive therapy alone.

For patients with severe aplastic anemia, authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 studies also found immunosuppressive therapy combined with EPAG had a better overall survival rate (pooled OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.2-2.5), but no significant differences in event-free survival rate. There were no differences in adverse events between the two groups

Authors of a systematic review of 10 cohort studies found combination EPAG with immunosuppressive therapies had a comparable overall response rate and 1-/2-year overall survival, but lower complete response rate when indirectly compared with haplo-HCT in the frontline treatment of patients with severe aplastic anemia.

In a cohort study of 118 patients with moderate aplastic anemia, an immunosuppressive therapy of cyclosporine alternately combined with levamisole, continued for 12 months after achieving maximal hematologic response, resulted in overall response rates of 100% and 86.8% for newly diagnosed and chronic disease groups, respectively. The 24-month progression-free survival was over 93% for both groups.

For patients preconditioned prior to hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT), the combination of reduced-dose cyclophosphamide, fludarabine, and ATG was superior to cyclophosphamide-ATG alone in reducing regimen-associated toxicities by over one half without increasing engraftment failure. Benefit of the addition of fludarabine to cyclophosphamide, ATG and single fraction total body irradiation was also demonstrated in another case series and was associated with improved survival.

In an RCT including 114 patients with refractory/relapsed acquired aplastic anemia, the 76 patients receiving EPAG+tacrolimus compared to the 38 patients receiving EPAG alone had a higher overall response rate at last follow-up of 60.5% vs. 34.2%.

Androgens (e.g., danazol) have been used in the past for marrow failure syndromes and are standard care for some constitutional syndromes but are regarded as less effective than immunosuppressive agents. Based on a meta-analysis of 43 RCTs including 2610 Chinese patients with non-severe aplastic anemia, adding cyclosporine to androgen therapy was more effective than androgen therapy alone. The most common adverse effects of combined therapy included hirsutism, tremor, gingiva hyperplasia, liver and renal function damage.

In several small studies, humanized anti-CD52 mAb alemtuzumab responses were comparable to cyclosporine-ATG for patients with refractory disease. However, alemtuzumab was not as effective for treatment-naive patients, resulting in early discontinuation of the trial.

In a RCT with 192 patients with newly diagnosed severe aplastic anemia who were not eligible for HCT, the addition of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor to ATG and cyclosporine did not change overall 6-year survival or event-free survival. However, patients randomized to the three drugs rather than ATG-cycosporine alone had fewer infectious episodes and hospitalization days.

There was no difference in overall survival, relapse or infections occurrence by adding hematopoietic growth factors to standard immunosuppressive therapy for patients with aplastic anemia based on a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs including 719 patients.

Romiplostim, a peptibody with thrombopoietin receptor agonist activity that stimulates endogenous thrombopoietin production, was shown in a phase II trial to achieve a platelet response in 10 of 33 evaluable patients at week 9 with 10 of 18 patients who eventually achieved a platelet response maintaining a response at 2-3 years. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in three (9%) of 35 patients, including grade 1 or 2 myalgia, fatigue, and dizziness. However, 17 (49%) of 35 patients had adverse events of grade 3 or higher and seven (20%) had serious adverse events (e.g., febrile neutropenia, cataract, retinal detachment) believed to be unrelated to treatment.
HCT is the definitive therapy.

Use of HCT is limited by the need for an HLA-matched donor and may have fatal complications such as graft-versus-host disease and infection. This is first-line therapy in patients younger than 45 years with an appropriate donor.

Evidence-based guidelines from the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy were published in 2024 for use of allogeneic HCT for severe aplastic anemia. The panel concluded the following: Bone marrow should be used as a graft source with use of rabbit over horse ATG for HCT conditioning. Fludarabine-containing regimens are preferred for patients at high risk of graft failure and those receiving matched unrelated or haploidentical donor transplant. The panel did not endorse the 40-year age cut-off for considering upfront HCT in adults, acknowledging that fit older patients may also benefit from HCT. The panel endorsed increased utilization of HCT by prioritizing matched unrelated or haploidentical donor HCT over immunosuppressive therapy in children and adults who lack a matched related donor. The panel suggested that either calcineurin inhibitor plus methotrexate or post-transplant cyclophosphamide-based graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis be used for matched related or matched unrelated donor recipients.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 studies with 577 patients undergoing haploidentical HCT found successful engraftment in 97.3% of patients (95% CI, 95.9-98.7). Grades II-IV acute and chronic graft-versus-host disease were reported in 26.6% and 25.0%, respectively and the pooled incidence of transplant-related mortality was 6.7% annually (95% CI, 4.0-9.4).

Because HLA-matched sibling or unrelated donors are not available in up to 70% of cases, alternate donors such as mismatched adult unrelated donors, haploidentical related donors, and umbilical cord blood stem cell products can be considered.

There was no difference between haploidentical HCT and matched unrelated donar HCT in 1-, 2-, or 3-year overall survival, failure-free survival, and engraftment based on a meta-analysis of 25 studies including 2252 patients with aplastic anemia. However, there were higher incidences of II-IV acute and chronic graft-versus-host and cytomegalovirus infection with haploidentical HCT.

Longer donor leukocyte telomere length appears to be associated with increased 5-year survival in patients who receive HCT for severe aplastic anemia; in one study, longer donor leukocyte telomere length was associated with 56% 5-year survival vs. 40% for those with shorter telomere length.

In a case series of 33 patients with acquired aplastic anemia with no HLA-matched donor who underwent a haploidentical transplantation with posttransplant cyclophosphamide, two-year overall survival was 78% and 2-year graft-versus-host disease-free survival was 63%.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 retrospective studies of alternative donor transplantation as an upfront treatment strategy in the absence of a matched sibling donor to immunosuppressive therapy in severe aplastic anemia found a 5-year overall survival rate of 89.2% vs. 82%, respectively; OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.85).

A 2020 guideline from The American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy provides recommendations for selecting adults with aplastic anemia for this type of therapy. This therapy is recommended after failure of a first immunosuppressive regimen in patients who lack HLA-matched donors. Cord blood transplantation is associated with a lower risk of chronic graft-versus-host disease.

In a phase 2 trial of 26 patients with refractory severe aplastic anemia, cord blood transplantation was followed by engraftment in 23 patients (88%) and 23 were alive at one year (88.5% overall survival rate). This differs significantly from the expected 20% survival. Cumulative incidences of grade II-IV acute and chronic graft-versus-host disease were 45.8% and 36%, respectively, over a median follow-up of 38.8 months.

A novel partial T-cell depleted transplant that infuses high numbers of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor-mobilized CD34+ selected peripheral blood stem cells combined with a bone marrow transplant-equivalent dose of non-mobilized donor T-cells is being tested that appears to reduce graft-versus-host disease.
Bone marrow may be a better source of cells and ATG-based regimens than peripheral blood stem cells because of lower incidence of graft-versus-host disease, based on a Latin American experience.
For patients in whom HCT is an option, transfusions should be limited to prevent sensitization.

Supportive treatment with frequent blood transfusions to a hemoglobin level greater than 8 mg/dL and/or a platelet level greater than 20,000/μL is often necessary. Base the need for frequent transfusions on the severity of the patient's symptoms and treatment strategy.
Treatment of infections and antimicrobial prophylaxis are important throughout the patient's course of treatment. C
Gene therapy may be considered in Fanconi Anemia. In a review of 3 trials including 9 patients, there was stabilization in blood lineages without any serious adverse effects at one-year follow-up.
If the aplastic anemia is not idiopathic, the offending agent should be discontinued.
If you suspect a patient has aplastic anemia, consider referral to a hematologist or oncologist.
Hospitalization will be necessary if the patient is neutropenic (absolute neutrophil count <500) and febrile.

Following treatment with immunosuppressive therapy, patients are at risk for solid tumors (head and neck), myelodysplastic syndromes, and acute leukemia. Patients receiving bone marrow transplantation are at an increased risk for solid tumors.

Patients with Fanconi anemia have a >500-fold incidence of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma relative to the general population. Authors of a review of treatments for these patients concluded that, when possible, surgical resection with curative intent should be the primary treatment.

In an RCT with 66 patients with severe aplastic anemia on immunosuppressive therapy with probable or suspected invasive fungal disease, use of empirical therapy was superior to diagnostic-driven therapy for effectiveness (78.1% vs. 47.1%, respectively).
More than 70% of patients with severe or very severe aplastic anemia who are left untreated will be dead within 1 year.
Increasing severity of aplastic anemia and increasing age are associated with a worse prognosis ().

In a Chinese retrospective study of 284 children with non-severe aplastic anemia (NSAA), most (69.7%) had persistent NSAA at a median follow-up of 43 months. Thirty-eight patients (13.4%) progressed to transfusion-dependent NSAA and 26 of these patients (9.2%) progressed to severe aplastic anemia.

In a systematic review, among people treated with immunosuppressive therapy, advanced age, severe aplastic anemia without very severe aplastic anemia, and combination anti-lymphocytic globulin plus cyclosporine A were factors associated with improved survival.

Among 1718 patients of median age 20 years treated with HCT for acquired severe aplastic anemia, overall 5-year survival was 70%. For survivors of matched sibling donor HCT, the cumulative incidence estimates of developing late effects were <3%. In contrast, for recipients of unrelated donor HCT, cumulative incidence of developing late effects exceeded 3% by 5 years. Late effects in this group included gonadal dysfunction in 10.5%, growth disturbance in 7.2%, avascular necrosis in 6.3%, hypothyroidism in 5.5%, and cataracts in 5.1%.
Frequent CBCs will be necessary to monitor the patient's response to treatment; also monitor cyclosporine levels weekly until a steady state is achieved.

A pediatric amendment to the British Society for Haematology adult guideline for aplastic anemia (2016) was developed by UK-based pediatric aplastic anemia medical experts and published in 2018. They recommend three tests prior to starting definitive therapy: chromosomal breakage test (diepoxybutane stress test) for Fanconi anemia, telomere length by flow cytometry-fluorescence in situ hybridization (Flow-FISH) to identify patients with dyskeratosis congenita (DC), and lymphocyte subset testing to identify the presence of B cell lymphopenia. If B cell lymphopenia or monocytopenia is identified, proceed with GATA2 genetic testing.

Once the diagnosis is confirmed, treatment preferences are: HCT from a matched sibling, second choice is immunosuppressive therapy with horse ATG prior to matched unrelated donor HCT followed by mismatched donor HCT (if no response to ATG or no matched donor available). If these do not work or are unavailable, they recommend treatment within a research trial or a second course of immunosuppressive therapy, androgens, alemtuzumab, eltrombopag or haploidentical or unrelated donor umbilical HCT.

In a feasibility trial of 57 young patients with severe aplastic anemia, 23 underwent randomization, 12 to matched unrelated donor bone marrow transplantation and 11 to immunosuppressive therapy. One transplant recipient experienced secondary graft failure, requiring a second procedure. Six of 11 randomized to immunosuppressive therapy responded, and five with refractory disease underwent successful salvage bone marrow transplantation.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 retrospective studies conducted in East-Asia with 491 young patients with severe aplastic anemia comparing haploidentical HCT to immunosuppressive therapy found no differences between groups in overall survival at 1, 3, 5, and 10 years but higher rates of failure-free survival in the HCT group at a cost of a higher incidence of infections (76% versus 45%, respectively) and high rates of acute and chronic graft versus host disease (54%; 95% Cl 43%∼64% and 43%; 95% CI 18%∼68%, respectively) for the haplo-HCT group.

This stands in contrast to results from a retrospective medical records study of children in South Korea with severe aplastic anemia of whom 23/42 underwent alternative donor HCT and 19/42 underwent front-line immunosuppressive treatment. Both estimated failure-free survival and event-free survival were significantly higher in the children who underwent alternative HCT (91.3% vs. 30.7% and 91.3% vs. 50.9%, respectively).

feature.caption: Classifying the Severity of Aplastic Anemia.
feature.feature_body:
Classification Definition 5-Year Survival, Stratified by Age (in Years)
Moderate Marrow cellularity <30% 20-49 = 86%
Absence of severe pancytopenia 50-59 = 72%
At least 2 of 3 blood elements below normal*
60 or older = 54%
Severe Marrow cellularity <25%, or 25%-50% with <30% residual 20-49 = 75%
Hematopoietic cells with at least 2 of 3 blood elements below normal*
50-59 = 52%
60 or older = 60%
Very severe Marrow cellularity <25%, or 25%-50% with <30% residual 20-49 = 49%
Hematopoietic cells with at least 2 of 3 blood elements below normal†
50-59 = 40%
60 or older = 21%
*neutrophils <0.5 × 109/L, platelets <20 × 109/L, and/or reticulocytes <20× 109/L; †neutrophils < 0.2 × 109/L, platelets <20 × 109/L, and/or reticulocytes <20× 109/L.
